steps: The deterministic projection (a,b)↦a is measurable. Pushing μ through it gives exactly its first marginal \(\mu_1=(\mathrm{fst})_\#\mu\). This assertion uses the actual input μ, not an arbitrary starting law with a different first marginal.

The product kernel a↦δₐ⊗κ(a,·) is measurable because it is the product of the identity kernel and the measurable conditional kernel. Composition with the deterministic projection gives K. Associativity of kernel/measure composition yields \[\mu K=\mu_1(\mathrm{id}\times\kappa)=\mu_1\otimes\kappa.\] The last expression is a measure–kernel composition product, not the independent product of μ₁ and a fixed marginal.

The supplied finite-measure disintegration identity now gives \[\mu K=\mu_1\otimes\kappa=\mu.\] It is justified by the standard-Borel, nonempty β and finite μ interface. No density, positivity, normalization to mass one or division by a marginal density is required. For μ=0 both sides are zero; this is invariant as a finite measure, not a probability law.

Conditional versions agree in their prescribed conditional meaning only for μ₁-almost every a. Replacing them on a μ₁-null set does not change the integrated identity. The chosen global Markov version still yields a legitimate mass-one update there, but no claim about conditional support or convergence from such exceptional starting states follows.

For lack of convergence take α={0,1}, β={∗} with discrete measurable structures and \(\mu=(\tfrac12\delta_0+\tfrac12\delta_1)\otimes\delta_\ast\). The update never changes either coordinate, so K is the identity kernel. Starting from \(\rho=\delta_{(0,\ast)}\), \[\rho K^n=\rho,\qquad d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\rho K^n,\mu)=\tfrac12\quad(n\ge0).\] Thus the actual invariant target does not imply uniqueness, irreducibility, mixing or convergence from a different first marginal.
